body:
What is hydrogen?

Hydrogen is the lightest chemical element. Its chemical symbol is H, while ordinary hydrogen gas consists of molecules with the formula H2. Under normal conditions, hydrogen is a colourless, odourless and highly flammable gas.

Hydrogen occurs abundantly in compounds such as water, hydrocarbons and organic matter. However, freely available hydrogen gas is relatively scarce. Therefore, hydrogen usually has to be produced by separating it from another substance, and this production requires energy or another source of chemical energy.

Hydrogen is an energy carrier: it can store energy obtained from another source and release that energy when used. It is not itself a primary renewable energy resource like sunlight or wind.

What makes hydrogen green?

Green hydrogen is hydrogen produced using renewable energy through an eligible low-emission production route. The most important route for this lesson is water electrolysis powered by renewable electricity. Solar or wind electricity operates an electrolyser, which splits water into hydrogen and oxygen.

The hydrogen can then be stored and supplied to a fertiliser factory, petroleum refinery, steel plant or suitable transport system. Its usefulness arises from the fact that energy originally obtained from renewable sources can be carried in chemical form and used at another time or place.

India's Green Hydrogen Standard also recognises eligible conversion of biomass using renewable energy. Thus, renewable-powered water electrolysis is the main example, but it is not the only route recognised under India's definition.

Why is green hydrogen important?

Solar and wind plants generate electricity, but some industries require hydrogen as a chemical feedstock rather than merely as a source of heat or electricity. A chemical feedstock is a substance consumed or transformed during the manufacture of another product. Hydrogen is already used to manufacture ammonia and to process petroleum products.

Replacing hydrogen obtained from fossil fuels with green hydrogen can reduce emissions associated with these existing industrial activities. Hydrogen may also help in applications where using electricity directly is difficult, such as certain industrial processes and selected forms of heavy transport.

Advantages and limitations

  • Energy storage: hydrogen can store renewable energy in chemical form for later use.
  • Industrial usefulness: it can replace conventionally produced hydrogen without changing hydrogen's underlying chemical function.
  • No carbon in the molecule: using pure hydrogen does not directly produce carbon dioxide from the hydrogen itself.
  • Production requirements: electricity, water, equipment and supporting infrastructure are needed to produce and deliver it.
  • Storage difficulty: hydrogen gas occupies a large volume at ordinary pressure, making storage and transport challenging.

Hydrogen is not automatically a clean fuel. Its environmental impact depends mainly on how it is produced and how much energy is used to process and transport it. Hydrogen made using coal-based electricity is not green merely because water was used as the raw material.

Hydrogen as a fuel and as a feedstock

These 2 uses must be distinguished. When hydrogen operates a fuel cell, its chemical energy is converted into electricity. When hydrogen is used to produce ammonia, it becomes part of another chemical compound. In petroleum refining, it participates in chemical reactions that improve the properties of petroleum products.

Consequently, green hydrogen should not be understood only as a replacement for petrol or diesel. Its role in fertilisers, refineries and other industries is equally important.

Prelims focus

  • Hydrogen's chemical symbol is H; hydrogen gas has the molecular formula H2.
  • Hydrogen is an energy carrier, not a primary renewable energy source.
  • Green hydrogen is commonly produced by water electrolysis using renewable electricity.
  • Hydrogen can be used both as an industrial feedstock and as an energy carrier.
  • Trap: Hydrogen does not become green simply because it produces no carbon dioxide at the point of use.

[Sources: NCERT, Resources and Development, Class 8, Chapter 3, Mineral and Power Resources, pp. 30–34 (2018–19); Press Information Bureau, Green Hydrogen: Emerging Pillar of India's Clean Energy Transition, sections Why Green Hydrogen and What Makes Hydrogen Green, 28 October 2026; Ministry of New and Renewable Energy, Green Hydrogen Standard for India, Office Memorandum No. 353/35/2022-NT, clause 1, 18 August 2023.]

title: Hydrogen: An Energy Carrier and the Meaning of Green Hydrogen

body:
Meaning of electrolysis

Electrolysis is a process in which an electric current drives a chemical reaction that would not proceed spontaneously in the same way under ordinary conditions. In water electrolysis, electricity supplies the energy required to break water into hydrogen and oxygen.

The overall balanced chemical equation is:

2H2O(l) → 2H2(g) + O2(g)

The equation shows that 2 molecules of water produce 2 molecules of hydrogen and 1 molecule of oxygen. Under the same temperature and pressure conditions, the volumes of hydrogen and oxygen collected are therefore in the ratio 2:1.

Main parts of an electrolyser

An electrolyser is the equipment used to carry out electrolysis. Its basic components are 2 electrodes, an electrolyte or ion-conducting membrane, an electrical supply and a means of keeping the product gases separate.

  • Cathode: the negative electrode in an electrolytic cell. Hydrogen gas is produced here.
  • Anode: the positive electrode in an electrolytic cell. Oxygen gas is produced here.
  • Electrolyte: a conducting medium that permits ions to move within the cell.
  • Separator or membrane: helps prevent hydrogen and oxygen from mixing while allowing the necessary movement of ions.

Production sequence

  1. Renewable electricity is obtained. Solar, wind or another eligible renewable source supplies electricity to the production system.
  2. Water is treated. Water is purified because dissolved impurities can interfere with electrolyser operation and shorten equipment life.
  3. Electrolysis takes place. Electricity drives the separation of water into hydrogen and oxygen.
  4. The gases are collected separately. Hydrogen is produced at the cathode and oxygen at the anode.
  5. Hydrogen is prepared for use. It is purified, dried and, when necessary, compressed for storage or delivery.

How much water is needed?

The chemical equation gives an important mass relationship. Approximately 9 kg of water is consumed to produce 1 kg of hydrogen and approximately 8 kg of oxygen. Since 1 litre of water has a mass close to 1 kg, the theoretical minimum water requirement is about 9 litres per kg of hydrogen.

Actual freshwater withdrawal may be higher because water purification, cooling and other plant operations can require additional water. The figure of 9 litres is therefore a basic chemical requirement, not a guarantee of total water consumption at every plant.

Alkaline and PEM electrolysis

FeatureAlkaline electrolysisPEM electrolysis
Ion-conducting mediumAlkaline electrolyte, commonly based on potassium hydroxideSolid proton-exchange membrane
Main moving ionHydroxide ion, OH−Hydrogen ion, H+
Common featureProduces hydrogen and oxygen from water using electricityProduces hydrogen and oxygen from water using electricity

Other electrolyser technologies also exist, but their basic purpose remains the same: to use energy to separate water into hydrogen and oxygen.

Water electrolysis is not the same as brine electrolysis

In the chlor-alkali process, electricity passes through an aqueous solution of sodium chloride, called brine. The important products are sodium hydroxide, chlorine and hydrogen. Hydrogen is released at the cathode, but chlorine is released at the anode.

By contrast, in the water-electrolysis process considered for green hydrogen, the intended gaseous products are hydrogen and oxygen. The input material and reaction products must therefore be checked before identifying an industrial electrolysis process.

Electrolyser: electricity is consumed to make hydrogen. Fuel cell: hydrogen is consumed to generate electricity. These are opposite energy-conversion directions.

Prelims focus

  • Overall reaction: 2H2O → 2H2 + O2.
  • Hydrogen forms at the negative cathode; oxygen forms at the positive anode.
  • Hydrogen and oxygen are produced in a 2:1 volume ratio under identical conditions.
  • About 9 litres of water are chemically required for 1 kg of hydrogen.
  • Alkaline electrolysis conducts hydroxide ions; PEM electrolysis conducts hydrogen ions.
  • Trap: Brine electrolysis produces chlorine at the anode, not oxygen as the principal anode product.

[Sources: NCERT, Science, Class 10, Chapter 1, Chemical Reactions and Equations, Activity 1.7 and Figure 1.6, pp. 9–10; Chapter 2, Acids, Bases and Salts, section 2.4.3, p. 30; NCERT, Science, Class 8, Chapter 14, Chemical Effects of Electric Current, pp. 176–178 (2018–19); U.S. Department of Energy, Hydrogen Production: Electrolysis, section How Do Electrolyzers Work? (accessed 16 November 2026); Press Information Bureau, Green Hydrogen: Emerging Pillar of India's Clean Energy Transition, section How Is Green Hydrogen Produced?, 28 October 2026.]

title: Water Electrolysis: How Green Hydrogen Is Produced

body:
Why are different colours used for hydrogen?

Hydrogen gas itself is colourless. Terms such as green, grey and blue hydrogen are labels for different production pathways. They indicate the energy source, raw material or emission-control method involved in making the hydrogen.

These labels are widely used, but their meanings are not completely uniform across all countries and publications. For an examination, the method of production is more important than memorising a colour without its explanation.

Major hydrogen colour classifications

LabelMain production routeImportant distinction
GreenRenewable-powered water electrolysis; eligible renewable biomass routesLow-emission pathway using renewable energy
GreyCommonly natural-gas reforming without effective carbon captureCarbon dioxide from production is generally released
BlueFossil-based hydrogen production with carbon capture and storage or utilisationSome associated carbon dioxide is captured; emissions are not necessarily zero
Brown or blackCoal gasificationCoal is the principal feedstock; emissions are typically high without capture
PinkWater electrolysis using nuclear electricityElectricity is low-carbon but not classified as renewable energy
TurquoiseMethane pyrolysisMethane is split into hydrogen and solid carbon

Steam methane reforming is an important conventional way of producing hydrogen from natural gas. Without adequate emission controls, the resulting hydrogen is generally called grey hydrogen. If a fossil-based process incorporates carbon capture, the hydrogen is commonly described as blue; its remaining emissions depend on factors such as capture effectiveness and methane leakage.

In methane pyrolysis, methane is converted into hydrogen and solid carbon rather than directly producing carbon dioxide as the principal carbon product. The resulting climate impact still depends on energy inputs, methane emissions and the handling of solid carbon.

Some sources also use additional labels, such as yellow hydrogen for particular electricity-based routes and white hydrogen for naturally occurring geological hydrogen. These extra colour conventions are less uniform. They should not override the actual method of production.

Solar electricity is not the same as coal electricity. Electrolysis powered by renewable solar electricity can be green. Electrolysis powered by coal-based electricity cannot be assumed green simply because the same electrolyser and water are used.

India's formal definition of green hydrogen

On 18 August 2023, the Ministry of New and Renewable Energy (MNRE) notified the Green Hydrogen Standard for India.

Under this standard, green hydrogen is hydrogen produced using renewable energy, including eligible production through electrolysis or conversion of biomass. Renewable electricity stored in an energy-storage system or banked with the grid can also qualify in accordance with applicable regulations.

The standard sets a maximum of 2 kg of carbon dioxide equivalent per kg of hydrogen for the specified non-biogenic greenhouse-gas emissions, calculated as an average over the preceding 12 months.

For electrolytic hydrogen, the specified assessment covers emissions associated with water treatment, electrolysis, gas purification, drying and hydrogen compression. Thus, India's standard does not require the measured emissions of every qualifying project to be exactly zero.

Who is responsible for verification?

The 2023 standard identifies the Bureau of Energy Efficiency (BEE) as the nodal authority for accreditation of agencies responsible for monitoring, verification and certification of green-hydrogen production projects. MNRE specifies the relevant framework and methodology.

The distinction between a colour label and a formal standard is important. A label such as green describes the intended production pathway, whereas the notified Indian standard specifies eligibility conditions and an emissions ceiling.

Prelims focus

  • Grey hydrogen is commonly produced from natural gas without effective carbon capture.
  • Blue hydrogen is fossil-based hydrogen produced with carbon capture.
  • Pink hydrogen uses nuclear electricity; green hydrogen uses renewable energy.
  • India's Green Hydrogen Standard was notified by MNRE on 18 August 2023.
  • The Indian emissions ceiling is 2 kg CO2-equivalent per kg H2, averaged over 12 months.
  • BEE is the nodal authority for accreditation of monitoring, verification and certification agencies.
  • Trap: Green hydrogen under India's standard is not restricted exclusively to water electrolysis; eligible biomass conversion is also included.

[Sources: Ministry of New and Renewable Energy, Green Hydrogen Standard for India, Office Memorandum No. 353/35/2022-NT, clauses 1–3, 18 August 2023; Centre for High Technology, Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas, Green Hydrogen, slide Colours of Hydrogen, available through the Petroleum and Natural Gas Regulatory Board, January 2025; Press Information Bureau, Green Hydrogen: Emerging Pillar of India's Clean Energy Transition, sections What Makes Hydrogen Green and Regulations and Standards, 28 October 2026.]
